title: ANOVA Decomposition and the F Test from R²
breadcrumb: Regression → Inference in the linear model → ANOVA and the overall F test
engineName: F is a ratio of per-degree-of-freedom averages; written in R² it is [R²/(k − 1)] / [(1 − R²)/(n − k)]
objectives: Build the ANOVA table with the correct degrees of freedom k − 1, n − k and n − 1.
Write F in terms of R², n and k, and check it against the mean-square ratio.
Use F = t² and R² = r² in simple regression, and the F-to-R² inversion.
State why the unbiased estimator of σ² is RSS/(n − k) and why TSS/(n − 1) is not.
Interpret a high R² with a non-significant F, and a low R² with a significant F.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Check the sums of squares, the F distribution, the null hypothesis and the residual degrees of freedom.

ask.q: What do TSS, RegSS and RSS each measure, and how do they relate?

body: A regression splits the variation in y into two parts. One part is explained by the fitted line. The rest is the residual. The analysis of variance is the bookkeeping that records those two parts, divides each by its degrees of freedom, and compares them with a ratio.

Q9 of the June paper asked for that ratio written in terms of R² alone, with the degrees of freedom in the right places. The answer was marked A where the key is B. The two options differ by where k − 1 and n − k sit, which is a verification slip, not a method gap. This lesson therefore builds the F ratio from the sums of squares first, then rewrites it in R², and checks the result on numbers.
No symbol is introduced before the case it names. The five-student data of topic 6.1 are used again: x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5.

items.ask: Define TSS, RegSS and RSS and state how they relate in a model with an intercept.
items.recall: TSS = Σ(y − ȳ)², RegSS = Σ(ŷ − ȳ)², RSS = Σ(y − ŷ)², and TSS = RegSS + RSS.
refresh: TSS is the total variation of y around its mean. RegSS is the variation of the fitted values around the same mean. RSS is what the fitted values fail to explain. For the five-student data: TSS = 6, RegSS = 3.6, RSS = 2.4.
The identity TSS = RegSS + RSS is Pythagoras on the right-angled triangle from topic 6.1. It needs the column of ones in X; without an intercept the centring no longer works.

items.recall: The ratio of two independent chi-squares, each divided by its degrees of freedom.
refresh: If A ~ χ²(a) and B ~ χ²(b) are independent, then (A/a)/(B/b) follows an F distribution with (a, b) degrees of freedom. Numerator degrees of freedom come first.
F is never negative and is skewed to the right. A large value says the numerator average is much bigger than the denominator average.

items.ask: What does the overall F test test?
items.recall: H₀: all slope coefficients are zero, against at least one non-zero.
refresh: The model has k coefficients, one of them the intercept. The overall test asks whether the k − 1 slopes could all be zero, which would make the regression no better than a constant.
Reject when F exceeds the upper 5% point of F(k − 1, n − k). Failing to reject means the data do not distinguish the model from a flat line; it does not prove the slopes are zero.

items.ask: How many degrees of freedom does the residual sum of squares carry?
refresh: From topic 6.1: the residual vector lives in a space of dimension tr(M) = n − k. For five observations and two coefficients that is 3.
The regression sum of squares carries k − 1, because the fitted values around their mean live in a space of dimension tr(H) − 1 = k − 1. The total carries n − 1, and (k − 1) + (n − k) = n − 1.

scenes.title: Splitting the variation, then comparing averages
scenes.objective: Describe the ANOVA split and why the F ratio compares per-degree-of-freedom averages.
body: The variation in y is the sum of squared distances from its mean. Fit a line and that total splits in two: what the line explains and what it leaves. If the line is useless, the explained part is only what chance would produce, and its average per degree of freedom is about the same as the residual's average per degree of freedom.

That is why the test is a ratio of averages. Each sum of squares is divided by the number of independent directions it covers: k − 1 for the regression, n − k for the residual. Under the null both averages estimate σ², so their ratio hovers around 1. A ratio well above 1 says the line is explaining more than chance would.
R² is the explained share of the total, RegSS/TSS. Because RegSS = R²·TSS and RSS = (1 − R²)·TSS, TSS cancels from the ratio. F depends on the data only through R², n and k.

scenario.teaser: A line that explains 60% of the variation, and still is not significant.
scenario.title: R² of 0.6 with five points
body: For the five-student data, x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 2, 4, 5, 4, 5, the total variation is TSS = 6. The fitted line explains RegSS = 3.6 of it, so R² = 3.6/6 = 0.6, and leaves RSS = 2.4.

Sixty per cent sounds like a good fit. The F ratio says otherwise. The regression carries k − 1 = 1 degree of freedom and the residual carries n − k = 3, so F = (3.6/1)/(2.4/3) = 3.6/0.8 = 4.5. The 5% critical value of F(1, 3) is 10.128. The observed 4.5 is far below it, with a p-value of 0.124.

With only five points a line can fit well by luck. The test accounts for that by asking how large a ratio chance alone produces when there are just three residual degrees of freedom. The answer is: large, so 4.5 is unremarkable.
scenario.q: If the same R² of 0.6 came from n = 50 observations, would F be bigger or smaller than 4.5?
scenario.answer: Bigger. F = (0.6/1)/(0.4/48) = 72, because dividing by n − k = 48 instead of 3 makes the residual average small. The same fit is far stronger evidence with more data.

ask.q: Why can R² be high while the overall F test fails to reject?
ask.nudge: Count the residual degrees of freedom.

scenes.title: A small sample needs a large correlation
scenes.objective: See that in simple regression the F test is a test on r², and find how large r must be at n = 5.

viz.caption: Set n = 5. The null density of r is a semicircle, and the 5% two-sided critical value is |r| = 0.878.

body: In simple regression R² equals the square of the correlation r between x and y, and F equals the square of the slope's t statistic. So the F test is a test on r. The picture shows the distribution of r when the true correlation is zero.

Set n = 5. The 5% critical value is |r| = 0.878, so the critical R² is 0.771. The five-student data have r = 0.775, so R² = 0.6 sits inside the acceptance region. Move n up to 20 and the critical |r| drops to about 0.44.
Nothing about the line changed between those two sample sizes. Only the amount of evidence changed.

ask.q: At n = 5 what R² is needed for significance at 5%?
ask.nudge: Square the critical |r| you read off.

scenes.title: The ANOVA table and F in R² form
scenes.objective: State the table, the F ratio and its R² form.

blocks.body:
Source        SS       df       MS                F
Regression    RegSS    k − 1    RegSS/(k − 1)     MSR/MSE
Residual      RSS      n − k    RSS/(n − k) = s²
Total         TSS      n − 1

blocks.h: F in terms of R²   (the form asked in Q9)
blocks.body:
F = [R²/(k − 1)] / [(1 − R²)/(n − k)]
  = (R²/(1 − R²)) · ((n − k)/(k − 1))
with (k − 1, n − k) degrees of freedom.

RegSS = R²·TSS and RSS = (1 − R²)·TSS. Substituting, the TSS in the numerator and the TSS in the denominator divide out, leaving the ratio above. The numerator is divided by k − 1, the denominator by n − k, and these must not be swapped: the first counts the slopes, the second counts the leftover.
For one regressor, k = 2: F has (1, n − 2) degrees of freedom and F = t², where t is the slope's t statistic. Also R² = r², the squared correlation of x and y.
If R² = 0 then F = 0. As R² approaches 1 the denominator goes to 0 and F goes to infinity. F is increasing in R² for fixed n and k.

flow.title: From R² to the decision
flow.alt: A top-to-bottom flow. Take R squared, n and k. Form F as R squared over k minus 1 divided by 1 minus R squared over n minus k. Compare with the upper 5 percent point of F with k minus 1 and n minus k degrees of freedom. Reject if larger.

nodes.label: Compare with F(k − 1, n − k) upper point
F larger: reject H₀, some slope is not zero

flow.note: Two things go wrong in practice: swapped degrees of freedom, and n used where n − k belongs.

scenes.title: Why the ratio is an F: two quadratic forms
scenes.objective: Explain the distribution of F under H₀ and what the mean squares estimate.

blocks.h: The two sums of squares as quadratic forms
blocks.body: Let J = 11′/n be the matrix that averages. Then TSS = y′(I − J)y, RegSS = y′(H − J)y, RSS = y′My. With an intercept, J is part of H, so H − J is symmetric idempotent with trace k − 1. M has trace n − k.
(H − J)M = HM − JM = 0 − 0 = 0, because HM = 0 and JM = 0 (J's direction lies in X). Two quadratic forms in normal errors whose matrices multiply to zero are independent.
When all slopes are zero, (H − J)Xβ = 0, so RegSS = u′(H − J)u, and RegSS/σ² ~ χ²(k − 1). RSS/σ² ~ χ²(n − k) always. Independent, so F = [RegSS/(k − 1)]/[RSS/(n − k)] ~ F(k − 1, n − k).

E(MSE) = σ² always.
E(MSR) = σ² + β′X′(H − J)Xβ/(k − 1), which is σ² only under H₀.
So F is near 1 under H₀ and larger when slopes are non-zero.

TSS/(n − 1) is not unbiased for σ² when slopes are non-zero. In the five-student set-up with σ² = 4, slope 0.5 and Sxx = 10, E(TSS/(n − 1)) = 4 + 0.25 × 10/4 = 4.625. A simulation of 200,000 samples gave 4.626.
For a single coefficient the partial F equals the square of its t statistic. In a check on random data with n = 20, k = 4 the partial F and t² agreed to eight digits.

scenes.title: On your own — F from R² with n and k
scenes.objective: Apply the R² form to a new case and check it.
scenes.problem: A regression with n = 20 observations and k = 4 coefficients has R² = 0.9. Find F and decide at 5%, given the upper 5% point of F(3, 16) is 3.239.
hints: Direction: write down the degrees of freedom first: k − 1 on top, n − k below.
Next step: compute R²/(1 − R²) = 9, then multiply by (n − k)/(k − 1) = 16/3.
scenes.answer: F = 48, far above 3.239, so reject H₀.
scenes.check: R²/(1 − R²) = 9; times 16/3 gives 48, and F must exceed that 9 because the factor 16/3 is above 1.

scenario.teaser: A fit that explains one per cent of the variation, and the test says it matters.
scenario.title: R² of 0.01 and n = 1000
body: A study regresses an outcome on one predictor using 1000 observations. R² is 0.01, so the predictor explains one per cent of the variation. A colleague calls the result trivial.

The overall F is (0.01/1)/(0.99/998) = 10.08. The 5% critical value of F(1, 998) is 3.85, so the test rejects comfortably. Both statements are correct. R² measures how much of the variation is explained. F measures whether the explained part could be chance.
With a thousand observations a weak but real effect is detectable. Statistical significance tells you the effect is not zero, and R² tells you how much it matters. Neither replaces the other.
scenario.q: Which of R² and F says the effect is real, and which says it is large?
scenario.answer: F says it is real (not zero). R² says how large a share of the variation it explains, which here is small.

solution.why: This is where Q9's options differ, so fix them first.

scenes.title: Six statements
scenes.objective: Spot the wrong versions of the F formula and its interpretation.
scenes.intro: Decide true or false on all six before revealing any.

items.claim: With R² = 0.6, n = 5, k = 2, swapping the degrees of freedom gives the right F.
items.why: The correct F is 4.5. Swapping gives (0.6/3)/(0.4/1) = 0.5.

items.claim: F = R²/(1 − R²) is enough, with no degrees-of-freedom factors.
items.why: That gives 1.5 for the five-student data. It leaves out the factor (n − k)/(k − 1) = 3.

items.claim: In simple regression F is the square of the slope's t statistic.
items.why: For the five-student data t = 2.1213 and t² = 4.5 = F.

items.claim: A significant F means every slope is non-zero.
items.why: It means at least one is. The overall test cannot say which.

items.claim: TSS = RegSS + RSS holds even for a model with no intercept.
items.why: The centring needs the column of ones in X. Without it the decomposition does not hold in this form.

items.claim: The unbiased estimator of σ² is RSS/(n − k).
items.why: E(RSS) = σ²(n − k), from tr(M) in topic 6.1.

scenes.title: Transfer — recover R² from a reported F
scenes.objective: Invert the F formula, a direction the lesson has not shown.
scenes.problem: A report gives F = 66.7365 on (3, 16) degrees of freedom. Find R².
hints: Direction: you know F, k − 1 = 3 and n − k = 16, and want R².
Method: write F = (R²/(1 − R²))·(16/3) and solve for R²/(1 − R²).
Next step: if R²/(1 − R²) = x, then R² = x/(1 + x).
scenes.check: F is huge, so R² must be close to 1.

solution.why: A common wrong step is F/(F + 16) = 0.807, which forgets the (k − 1) factor.

blocks.body: The quadratic forms y′Hy and y′My come from topic 6.1. Their distribution under normality uses the chi-square count n − k from there.
Topic 6.4 reads R² and adjusted R² off the same table and compares nested models with an F test built the same way. Topic 6.5 explains why a significant F can sit beside insignificant t values.
Single-factor and two-factor designed experiments use the same table but belong to the design-of-experiments module. This lesson treats only the regression case.

scenes.title: Extension — F as a partial F for one restriction
scenes.objective: Show that a single-restriction F equals t².

blocks.body: Drop the j-th regressor. The extra residual sum of squares is RSS_r − RSS_f, with one degree of freedom.
(RSS_r − RSS_f)/(RSS_f/(n − k)) = b_j²/(s²·c_jj), where c_jj is the j-th diagonal of (X′X)⁻¹. The right side is the square of the t statistic b_j/(s√c_jj).
On a random data set with n = 20 and k = 4 the partial F was 3.6614 and the squared t statistic was 3.6614.
